title: Effect of reaustenitization on grain refinement and mechanical properties in multipass Fe-10Ni weld metal
abstract: Abstract This study investigated the effect of supercritical reheats on the grain refinement mechanism, martensitic substructure, hardness, and impact toughness in a multipass gas metal arc weld (GMAW) of Fe-10Ni steel weld metal. Prior-austenite grain (PAG) size, effective grain size, high-angle grain boundary (HAGB) density, hardness, and Charpy V-notch (CVN) energy were quantified. Reaustenitization of the coarse-grained dendritic as-solidified microstructure produced substantially refined equiaxed grains, reducing PAG and effective grain sizes respectively by up to two orders of magnitude and fourfold, while significantly increasing HAGB density. The extent of refinement was governed by peak reaustenitization temperature and time above A C3 , controlled by cooling rate. Subsequent supercritical and intercritical reheats of simulated CGHAZ refined the grain size to levels comparable to single supercritical reheats. Grain growth during austenitization was governed by boundary migration in the absence of carbide pinning, related to low weld metal carbon content and the carbide formers, V and Mo, being tied in weld metal oxide particles. A critical HAGB density of ~0.57 µm⁻ 1 , corresponding to PAG ~31 µm and effective grain size ~3 µm, marked the transition to coarse martensite formation. Weld metal hardness was relatively insensitive to reaustenitization reheats. In contrast, reaustenitized conditions showed improved CVN energy relative to the as-welded condition, with superior toughness in 1000 °C reheats attributed to refined grains, higher HAGB density, and absence of coarse martensite. These results demonstrate that reaustenitization effectively refines the Fe-10Ni weld metal microstructure, increases HAGB density, suppresses coarse martensite, and governs impact toughness variability in multipass welds.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: High-nickel steels have long been pursued for structural applications requiring a combination of high strength and exceptional low-temperature toughness. Among these materials, Fe-10 wt.% Ni steel has emerged as a promising candidate for naval structural applications due to its high hardenability, low carbon content, and excellent resistance to brittle fracture. The addition of approximately 10 wt.% Ni promotes martensitic transformation over a wide range of cooling rates while suppressing the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature, enabling ultimate tensile strengths exceeding 125 ksi while retaining high impact toughness at subzero temperatures [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 – 4 ]. In the base material, these properties are further enhanced through a three-step quenching–lamellarizing–tempering (QLT) heat treatment, which promotes retained austenite films between martensite laths and contributes to transformation-induced plasticity and improved energy absorption during deformation [ 1 ,  5 ,  6 – 7 ].

Gas metal arc welding (GMAW) is a commonly used joining method for thick-section components in ship construction. Welding of thick plate typically requires multiple passes, generating thermal cycles that reheat previously transformed regions. To achieve welds with strength and toughness comparable to the Fe-10Ni base material, a Fe-10Ni-based solid wire electrode was developed for GMAW applications [ 8 ,  9 ]. Unlike the base metal, Fe-10Ni weld metal does not undergo QLT heat treatment and therefore transforms predominantly to martensite with a significantly lower fraction of retained austenite [ 8 ]. In GMAW spray transfer (GMAW-s), commonly used shielding gas compositions, such as 98% Ar–2% O 2 , promote oxide formation in the weld metal, which has been shown to reduce impact toughness by increasing void nucleation sites during fracture.

Barrick and DuPont investigated the influence of grain size and oxide content on the impact toughness of Fe-10Ni weld metal and demonstrated that grain size is an important contributor to toughness variability [ 10 ]. However, their study relied primarily on short isothermal hold-time experiments at a limited number of peak temperatures to reproduce specific grain sizes. As a result, the influence of realistic welding thermal cycles on grain size evolution has not been fully established. During multipass welding, repeated reheating can result in both grain coarsening and refinement depending on the thermal cycle characteristics, including the peak temperature attained and the cooling rate. The extent to which these parameters govern prior-austenite grain size (PAG), effective grain size, and the resulting impact toughness in Fe-10Ni weld metal remains insufficiently quantified.

Grain growth modeling has been widely used to predict grain size under both isothermal heat treatments [ 11 ,  12 – 13 ] and non-isothermal welding thermal cycles [ 14 ,  15 – 16 ]. Early Arrhenius-type formulations related grain growth to temperature and time [ 17 ], whereas later models incorporated effects of initial grain size and material kinetic constants [ 11 ]. Welding-specific approaches, such as those developed by Ashby and Easterling, integrated grain growth kinetics over entire thermal cycles to capture non-isothermal behavior [ 18 ], with subsequent refinements accounting for the evolution of grain boundary pinning particles during heating were introduced by Andersen and Grong [ 12 ]. While these models are important, their application requires experimentally determined kinetic and mobility parameters that are specific to the alloy system and thermal history.

Prior studies of multipass grain refinement in Ni steels have focused on the heat-affected zone (HAZ) rather than the weld metal itself. For example, Morris reported significant refinement of the HAZ microstructure in multipass 9–12% Ni steel welds [ 19 ], while Ma et al. showed that impact-trailed welding can induce recrystallization during multipass welding of 8–11% Ni bearing austenitic stainless steels, leading to substantial HAZ grain refinement [ 20 ]. In contrast, little work has quantified the extent of grain refinement within multipass Fe-10Ni weld metal itself, particularly the transition from the coarse columnar as-welded structure to the refined reaustenitized microstructure. Previous work by the authors demonstrated that multipass welding of Fe-10Ni refines the majority of previously deposited weld layers through reheating, except within the deep finger-penetration regions characteristic of GMAW-s welds, where portions of the original columnar microstructure can persist [ 21 ]. However, the degree of refinement, as well as the influence of peak temperature and cooling rate on the resulting PAG and effective grain sizes, has not been quantitatively established. Consequently, a quantitative description of refinement and growth behavior in Fe-10Ni weld metal as a function of welding thermal cycle parameters remains lacking.

The objective of this study is to establish quantitative relationships between welding thermal history, grain size evolution, and mechanical properties in Fe-10Ni weld metal under conditions representative of multipass GMAW. To address this knowledge gap, this work (i) evaluates grain refinement during reaustenitization and subsequent grain growth under non-isothermal thermal cycles, (ii) quantifies the independent roles of peak temperature and cooling rate on PAG size and effective grain size and formation of detrimental constituents, and (iii) directly links these microstructural features to impact toughness. By integrating controlled thermal simulations with detailed microstructural characterization, this study provides a mechanistic framework for understanding impact toughness variability in multipass Fe-10Ni weld metal.

sections.heading: Experimental weld buildup
paragraphs: An Fe-10Ni weld buildup was deposited on a low carbon steel base plate using gas metal arc welding in spray transfer mode (GMAW-s) with a shielding gas of 98% Ar–2% O 2 . The resulting buildup measured 254 mm in length, 152 mm in width, and 76 mm in height and is displayed in Fig.  1 . Cylindrical Gleeble specimens and Charpy V-Notch (CVN) bars were extracted in the transverse direction from the weld buildup. To minimize the influence of base plate dilution, only weld metal material from the upper 52.4 mm of the buildup was utilized for sample extraction. The chemical composition of the undiluted weld metal is provided in Table  1 . sections.heading: Thermal simulations
paragraphs:
Round specimens (6.35 mm diameter × 63 mm length) were subjected to isothermal simulations to peak temperatures above the A C1  (686 °C) and A C3  (726 °C) of Fe-10Ni weld metal [ 21 ] using a Gleeble™ 3800 thermo-mechanical simulator. The first set of simulations was conducted under simplified isothermal conditions to establish the intrinsic grain growth behavior of Fe-10Ni weld metal. Specimens were heated to peak temperatures of 900 °C, 1100 °C, and 1350 °C and held for 1, 60, and 300 s using a 100 °C/s heating rate and an average cooling rate of 70 °C/s (Table  2 ). These tests provided a baseline understanding of grain coarsening as a function of temperature and hold time.

To evaluate grain size evolution under realistic welding conditions, non-isothermal simulations were conducted in the Gleeble using calibrated thermal histories from Fe-10Ni bead-on-plate weld models detailed in a previous publication [ 21 ]. The Gleeble thermal simulations incorporated three heat inputs: 25, 40, and 55 kJ/in which had t 8/5  cooling rates of 62, 38, and 27.2 °C/s. For each cooling rate, samples were heated to peak temperatures of 1000 °C, 1100 °C, 1200 °C, and 1350 °C (Table  2 ). Figure  2  shows a representative set of thermal histories for the 62 °C/s cooling rate. The total time spent above A C3  for all peak temperatures and cooling rates is displayed in Table  3 . Fig. 2 Schematic illustration of  thermal histories experienced during simulated weld thermal cycles at a cooling rate of 62 °C/s Table 3 Total time spent above A C3  for each peak temperature (°C) and cooling rate Peak temperature (°C) Cooling rates/times above A C3  (s)
 62 °C/s 38 °C/s 27.2 °C/s 1000 2.74 4.6 6.7 1100 3.53 5.47 7.65 1200 4.06 5.91 7.83 1350 4.18 6.77 6.93

Oversized Charpy V-Notch (CVN) specimens (11 × 11 × 55 mm) were then subjected to thermal simulations in the Gleeble using the same calibrated thermal histories to replicate regions characteristic of the fine grain heat-affected zone (FGHAZ) (1000 °C) and coarse grain heat-affected zone (CGHAZ) (1350 °C) under fast (62 C/s) and slow (27C/s) cooling rates [ 9 ].

A third set of Gleeble simulations was conducted to evaluate the influence of reheating during multipass welding on grain growth and refinement. In these experiments, specimens were initially heated to 1350 °C, held for 1 s, and cooled. The specimens were then reheated to 1350 °C, followed by secondary peak temperatures of 1000 °C or 700 °C. The 700 °C condition lies within the intercritical range for this weld metal, between A C1  = 686 °C and A C3  = 726 °C [ 21 ]. All Gleeble simulations employed a heating rate of 100 °C/s and an average cooling rate of 70 °C/s. A complete summary of all thermal simulation parameters is provided in Table  2 .

sections.heading: Mechanical testing
paragraphs: Specimens subjected to non-isothermal simulations were cross-sectioned at the thermocouple locations and hardness tested. Microhardness measurements were performed using a LECO LM-100AT tester with a 200 g load and a 250 µm indent spacing, with a total of 10 indents per sample. Standard 10 × 10 × 55 mm CVN specimens extracted from non-reaustenitized (as-welded) weld metal were machined to evaluate the baseline impact toughness of Fe-10Ni weld metal. Oversized CVN specimens subjected to thermal simulations were subsequently machined to standard 10 × 10 × 55 mm subsize dimensions. A V-notch was positioned at the thermocouple location to ensure alignment between the microstructure of interest and the fracture plane. CVN testing was conducted in accordance with ASTM E23 at 0 °F (−17.8 °C) and three samples were tested for each condition [ 22 ].

sections.heading: Metallurgical characterization
paragraphs: All isothermal and non-isothermal simulation specimens, together with the as-welded condition, were cross-sectioned and prepared using standard metallographic techniques. A final polish with 0.05-µm colloidal silica for 45 min was performed to enable characterization using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) with a ThermoFisher Quattro ESEM using a 400-nm step size. Raw patterns were saved and subsequently reindexed using the spherical indexing  in EDAX OIM Analysis v9 to improve indexing accuracy and angular resolution. Fe-10Ni weld metal transforms fully to martensite across a wide range of cooling rates [ 3 ]. Therefore, all samples contained a martensitic microstructure. To characterize the prior-austenite grains, PAG reconstruction was performed in OIM Analysis v9 using the Nishiyama-Wasserman austenite to ferrite orientation relationship. Grain size was quantified using the equivalent circle diameter (ECD) method, where grains were reconstructed using a 15° misorientation threshold and a minimum of five pixels per grain, in accordance with ASTM E2627 [ 23 ]. Five EBSD scans per condition were analyzed to obtain an average PAG grain size. The effective grain size was also calculated using the methodology reported by Ueji et al. [ 24 ]. For microstructural characterization, cross-sectioned samples were etched using a 2% Nital solution for 30 s and examined using a Thermo Scientific Apreo field-emission gun scanning electron microscope (FEG-SEM). Fractured CVN specimens were sectioned parallel to the crack propagation direction and prepared for EBSD. Maps were acquired along the fracture path using a 300-nm step size and were spherically reindexed. Inverse pole figure (IPF) maps, kernel average misorientation (KAM) maps, and grain boundary maps were generated for each condition.

sections.heading: Carbon replica analysis
paragraphs: Carbide extraction was performed using a carbon replica technique on the sample thermally cycled to 1000 °C at 62 °C/s cooling rate. The sample was cross-sectioned and etched using 2% Nital for 5 min. Acetone droplets were applied to the etched surface and covered with cellulose acetate tape. After drying, the tape was peeled off and carbon-coated to a thickness of approximately 50 nm using a carbon coater. The cellulose acetate was dissolved in acetone, releasing the carbon film that contained extracted carbides. The film was mounted on a transmission electron microscopy (TEM) grid and analyzed in a Tecnai T20 TEM using scanning TEM (STEM) imaging and energy-dispersive X ray spectroscopy (EDS). A detailed methodology on the carbon replica technique can be found here [ 25 ].

sections.heading: As-solidified weld metal
paragraphs: Figure  5 m and n present inverse pole figure (IPF) maps of the reconstructed PAGs for the as-welded condition. The microstructure is characterized by large, columnar prior-austenite grains with an average PAG size of 570 µm (Table  5 ). Figure  5 m shows the corresponding grain boundary map, highlighting the very low high-angle grain boundary (HAGB) density of this condition (0.20 µm⁻ 1 ), which results in a coarse effective grain size of 10.04 ± 0.52 µm (Table  5 ). Additionally, due to the coarse effective grain size and low HAGB density, the detrimental coarse martensite (CM) constituent is present and is indicated in Fig.  5 m. The hardness of this condition was investigated in a previous publication and showcased a hardness of 292 HV [ 21 ].

sections.heading: Isothermal grain growth
paragraphs:
Figure  3  and Table  4  present the average PAG size measured across all tested peak temperatures and hold times for the Fe-10Ni weld metal. At 900 °C, grain growth was minimal, with only a slight increase in average PAG size observed with increasing hold time, indicating negligible coarsening. In contrast, appreciable grain growth occurred at 1100 °C, with the largest increase occurring between the shortest and intermediate hold times. At 1350 °C, rapid grain coarsening occurred within the first second, followed by more gradual increases in PAG size at longer hold times. The PAG size values for all conditions are summarized in Table  4 . sections.heading: Non-isothermal grain growth
Effect of multiple reheats on grain size
paragraphs: Figure  9  displays how the PAG size and martensitic substracture change when the 1350 °C baseline condition is followed by a second thermal cycle to 1000 °C, 700 °C (intercritical). Figure  9  and Table  5  show that reheating Fe-10Ni weld metal to 1000 °C results in a substantial decrease in PAG size and effective grain size. Reheating to the intercritical temperature of 700 °C also refines the PAG and the effective grain sizes. The measured PAG and effective grain sizes are plotted in Fig.  4 a and b. The HAGB density of the multiple reheat conditions is shown in Fig.  7 . Fig. 9 IPF, and grain boundary maps showing PAG and martensitic substructure for  a  1350 °C,  b  1350 °C + 1000 °C, and  c  1350 °C + 700 °C

sections.heading: Grain size influence on mechanical properties
paragraphs: Figure  10  shows hardness as a function of cooling rate for the different peak temperatures. For a given cooling rate, hardness decreased with increasing peak temperature. For a given peak temperature, hardness increased with increasing cooling rate. Across all conditions, hardness ranged from approximately 303 to 325 HV 0.2 , indicating that grain size variations induced by peak temperature and cooling rate had only a minor effect on hardness. Similarly, the as-welded microstructure exhibited a hardness of 292 HV [ 21 ], slightly lower than that of the reheated conditions. Figure  11  presents the CVN impact energies measured at 0 °F for peak temperatures of 1000 °C and 1350 °C at cooling rates of 62 °C/s and 27.2 °C/s as well as the as-welded condition. For both peak temperatures, changes in cooling rate resulted in relatively small differences in CVN energy, while a larger difference was observed between the two peak temperature conditions. However, the as-welded condition, which had the largest PAG and effective grain size, performed the worst. Figure  12  shows the relationship between CVN energy and both effective grain size and PAG size for all tested conditions. Fig. 10 Hardness for different cooling rates for peak temperatures between 1000 and 1350 °C Fig. 11 Charpy V-notch impact energies for 1000 °C and 1350 °C peak temperatures for 62 and 27.2 °C/s cooling rates as well as the as-welded condition tested at 0 °F (−17.8 °C) Fig. 12 CVN impact energy measured at 0 °F plotted as a function of PAG size (bottom axis) and effective grain size (top axis) for Fe-10Ni weld metal

Having established the effects of grain size and cooling rate on the impact toughness of the thermally simulated Fe-10Ni weld metal, metallurgical characterization was conducted on the test samples. Because the 62 °C/s and 27.2 °C/s cooling rate conditions at each peak temperature exhibited similar CVN impact energies, only the 62 °C/s condition was examined for each peak temperature. Figure  13  presents IPF maps of the fracture path with high-angle grain boundaries overlaid, along with the corresponding KAM and HAGB maps. The KAM maps indicate a higher overall local misorientation in the 1000 °C condition, with an average KAM value of 0.88°, compared to 0.74° for the 1350 °C condition. The HAGB maps show a lower boundary density in the 1350 °C condition, consistent with the larger PAG and effective grain sizes. Fig. 13 EBSD IPF, KAM, and HAGB along the fracture surface for 62 °C/s cooling rate CVN samples at 1350 °C ( a – c ) and 1000 °C ( d – f ). Effective grain size (EFS). Maps were scanned using a 300-nm step size

sections.heading: Carbon carbide replicas
paragraphs: To investigate whether grain-pinning carbides such as VC were present due to the purposeful alloying of vanadium [ 9 ], the carbon replica technique was applied to the 1000 °C, 62 °C/s condition. Many particles were observed on the TEM grids, as shown in Fig.  14 a; however, they all appear to be oxides that detached from the matrix during the etching and carbon replica preparation process. No evidence of VC particles or any other carbides was found on the carbon replicas. The elemental maps in Fig.  14 c and d show that the oxide particles contain O, Mn, and Si, V and Mo. Fig. 14 STEM-EDS analysis of oxide particles identified from carbon replicas.  a  Carbon replica on TEM grid,  b  STEM image showing oxide particles, and  c – g  corresponding elemental maps illustrating the oxide composition

sections.heading: Grain growth behavior in Fe-10Ni weld metal
paragraphs: Supercritical reheating of the as-welded Fe-10Ni weld metal produced significant microstructural refinement to the coarse-grained as-welded condition, as shown in Fig.  5 . The as-welded microstructure is characterized by large columnar grains, whereas reheated conditions exhibit predominantly equiaxed prior-austenite grain morphologies, resulting from reaustenitization and subsequent grain nucleation during reheating [ 26 ]. This transformation is accompanied by an approximately two orders of magnitude reduction in average PAG size. A two to fourfold reduction in effective grain size is also observed, depending on the experienced supercritical peak temperature. In addition, HAGB density increases substantially, from 0.20 µm⁻ 1  in the as-welded condition to as high as 0.86 µm⁻ 1  in the most refined reaustenitized condition, reflecting the refinement of the as-welded grains then the subsequent transformation to martensite. Achieving such refinement during multipass welding of Fe-10Ni is critical, as prior work by Barrick and DuPont [ 10 ] demonstrated that large soldification grains retained in as-welded regions are highly detrimental to overall impact toughness. These refinement effects are governed primarily by the peak temperature and the duration of exposure above the A C3  temperature during reheating.

The extent to which this refined structure coarsens depends on the grain growth behavior during austenitization, which in Fe-10Ni weld metal is dominated by peak temperature with secondary influences from cooling rate and hold time that vary depending on the thermal regime. At higher peak temperatures of 1100 and 1350 °C, rapid grain growth occurs under isothermal conditions, with the majority of coarsening taking place within the first 60 s, followed by a clear plateau in grain size at longer hold times, as shown in Fig.  3 . This rapid initial coarsening is attributed to the strong temperature dependence of grain growth [ 13 ,  27 ]. Dong et al. reported similar plateauing in austenite grain size at longer hold times in SA-508 [ 28 ]. In contrast, at 900 °C, which is only slightly above the A C3  temperature of Fe-10Ni weld metal, grain growth is strongly suppressed, with only a minor increase in PAG size observed after 300 s. This behavior is consistent with grain boundary migration kinetics [ 26 ], where reduced kinetics at lower temperatures limit grain boundary migration despite extended hold times. This has been observed by studies that looked at the influence of hold times on grain growth in low carbon steels [ 29 ,  30 ].

Under non-isothermal conditions, the grain growth behavior of Fe-10Ni weld metal reflects the combined influence of peak temperature and cooling rate, with peak temperature remaining the dominant factor. Figure  4  shows that for peak temperatures between 1100 and 1350 °C, slower cooling rates resulted in larger PAG sizes due to the increased time spent above the A C3  temperature, as summarized in Table  3 . The extended duration in the fully austenitic regime provides additional time for grain boundary migration, allowing grains to coarsen and the average PAG size to increase. In contrast, at a peak temperature of 1000 °C, grain growth remained limited across all cooling rates, consistent with the suppressed grain boundary mobility observed under isothermal conditions at similar temperatures. These results indicate that cooling rate influences grain growth primarily by extending the duration of the fully austenitic regime, but only when the peak temperature is sufficiently high to activate significant grain boundary motion.

Similar trends have been reported in prior studies. Banerjee et al. showed that at lower peak temperatures, the influence of cooling rate on grain growth is diminished, whereas a more pronounced effect is observed at higher peak temperatures in low carbon steels [ 30 ]. Gu et al. likewise reported that in X100 pipeline steels the average PAG size increased significantly with increasing peak temperature under non-isothermal thermal cycles [ 31 ].

sections.heading: Effective grain size
paragraphs: This work showed that effective grain size increases with decreasing cooling rate and increasing peak temperature, with the most pronounced changes occurring at peak temperatures between 1100 and 1350 °C (Fig.  4 b). At these higher temperatures, coarsening of the PAGs leads to a reduction in the density of HAGB formed during martensitic transformation, resulting in a coarser martensitic substructure, as shown in Fig.  6 . In contrast, at a peak temperature of 1000 °C, the effective grain size remains relatively small and exhibits only minor sensitivity to cooling rate, consistent with the limited PAG growth observed under these conditions. Comparison of Fig.  4 a and b shows that increases in PAG size are accompanied by corresponding increases in effective grain size. These results demonstrate that effective grain size in Fe-10Ni weld metal is strongly coupled to PAG size under welding thermal cycles, and that refinement of the PAGs provides an effective means of refining the martensitic substructure.

To place these observations in context, it is necessary to consider how effective grain size is defined in martensitic steels and why it governs mechanical behavior more directly than PAG size alone. Fe-10Ni weld metal transforms to low carbon martensite upon cooling across a wide range of cooling rates. PAG breaks down into packets, which break down into blocks, which then break down into laths in low carbon martensite [ 32 ,  33 ]. In these steels, cleavage propagation occurs in the {100} crystallographic planes [ 34 ,  35 – 36 ], and the effective grain size is the distance between the boundaries where the {100} plane changes. It has been determined by Morris et al. [ 35 ] that the plane change occurs at martensite block boundaries, which are HAGBs. Wang et al. [ 34 ] show that packet boundaries, which are HAGBs, also deflect the propagation of cracks. HAGBs are boundaries that have a misorientation angle greater than 15° [ 24 ,  32 ]. Therefore, the effective grain size in martensitic steels is determined by the HAGBs (packets, blocks, PAG boundries) that can inhibit the propagation of cracks. EBSD grain boundary maps in Fig.  6  and the HAGB density plot in Fig.  7  corroborate this, with the density of HAGBs decreasing with decreasing cooling rates. This results in a larger effective grain size (Fig.  4 b), indicating a coarser martensitic substructure and a reduced boundary area per unit area.

In addition to influencing effective grain size, the reduction in HAGB density at higher peak temperatures and slower cooling rates also promotes the formation of CM. CM is characterized by large regions of martensite lacking HAGBs throughout the constituent, creating areas where cleavage cracks can easily propagate [ 2 ,  37 ,  38 – 39 ]. Barrick and Dupont attributed the presence of CM to the reduced impact toughness observed in GMAW multipass groove welds compared to the more refined gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW) groove welds. As shown in Fig.  6 , CM is predominantly observed in conditions associated with larger PAG sizes and coarser effective grain sizes, particularly for peak temperatures of 1200 and 1350 °C, and the as-welded condition, which has the largest effective grain size. In contrast, CM is absent at a peak temperature of 1000 °C for all cooling rates, consistent with the finer martensitic substructure and higher density of HAGB (Fig.  7 ) observed under these conditions. Using these observations together with the HAGB densities shown in Fig.  7 , a threshold HAGB density of approximately 0.58 µm⁻ 1  is identified, above which CM is not observed, and below which CM is present in Fe-10Ni weld metal. SEM images shown in Fig.  8 c and d showcase CM present at 1350 °C at slow and fast cooling rates, while Fig.  8 a and b showcase the refined microstructure of the 1000 °C with no CM present.

The empirical equations developed in Tables  6  and  7  for PAG and effective grain size as functions of cooling rate at supercritical reheat temperatures, when used together with HAGB density results, provide a useful framework for computational process–microstructure–property optimization in multipass Fe-10Ni welds. Using these relationships, grain size can be assigned to predicted thermal cycles from process simulations, enabling estimation of grain size distributions for given welding parameters. A similar approach was previously employed by the authors to assign hardness and microstructure distributions using empirically derived process–property relationships [ 21 ]. In this way, the combined use of grain size and HAGB density relationships enables identification of reheating conditions that promote refined microstructures and suppress CM formation, thereby supporting optimization of welding parameters to improve impact toughness in multipass Fe-10Ni welds.

sections.heading: Effect of multiple reheats on grain size
paragraphs: In multipass welding, it is important to understand the influence of repeated thermal cycles experienced by previously deposited weld metal as subsequent beads are deposited. Following the baseline 1350 °C condition, reheating to a lower peak temperature of 1000 °C resulted in significant refinement of both the PAG size and the effective grain size, as shown in Fig.  8 . This observation is consistent with the work of Hidalgo and Santofimia, who showed that the first refinement reheat produces the majority of the grain refinement, with additional reheats contributing only minor further refinement [ 32 ]. Similarly, Grange reported that reheating can be used to refine coarse PAGs and that the final grain size is largely independent of the initial grain size when the same heat-treatment temperature is used [ 40 ]. Applied to the present study from a multipass welding perspective, these findings indicate that the refined grain sizes achieved after a single reheat to a lower peak temperature will not change significantly after additional reheats to the same or similar peak temperature. The refinement observed at 1000 °C was significant enough that the final grain sizes closely matched those obtained from single-reheat simulations at 1000 °C with different cooling rates (Fig.  4 ). This allows this work to conclude that the single-reheat grain sizes measured above A C3  in this study provide a reliable indication of the final refined microstructure even after multiple reheats to the temperatures investigated here.

Reheating to the intercritical temperature range results in partial transformation to austenite and, upon cooling, retransformation to martensite. The microstructure consists of newly formed martensite and tempered martensite. However, based on the resultant PAG and effective grain sizes shown in Fig.  9 , reheating to the intercritical temperature range (700 °C) produces similar refinement to reheating to 1000 °C. This is significant as it shows that effective grain refinement does not require full reaustenitization; even intercritical reheating is sufficient to break up coarse grains and produce microstructures comparable to those formed at higher temperatures for this material.

sections.heading: Influence of grain size on mechanical properties
Hardness
paragraphs: Hardness in Fe-10Ni weld metal exhibits limited sensitivity to variations in grain size, as shown in Fig.  10 . For a given cooling rate, hardness decreased with increasing peak temperature, while for a fixed peak temperature, only a slight increase in hardness was observed with increasing cooling rate. The increase in hardness with cooling rate is attributed to the formation of a finer effective grain size due to the reduced time available for grain growth, leading to finer PAGs and a more refined martensitic substructure [ 41 ,  42 ]. These hardness variations are consistent with the differences in martensitic substructure shown in Fig.  6 . Faster cooling rates produce a finer effective grain size, as shown in Fig.  4 b, increasing the density of boundaries that contribute to strengthening. Although faster cooling promotes refinement of the effective grain size, this refinement does not translate to a significant increase in hardness.

The as-welded condition exhibited a hardness of 292 HV, whereas the single fully reaustenitized conditions showed a narrow hardness range of 303–325 HV 0.2 . This behavior contrasts with that of conventional martensitic steels, where hardness and tensile strength scale inversely with effective grain size [ 38 ,  41 ]. Ali et al. [ 41 ] reported that refining the effective grain size through faster cooling  increased YS, UTS, and hardness in ultrahigh-strength martensitic steels. Because hardness is empirically correlated with UTS [ 43 ], the negligible hardness variation in Fe-10Ni weld metal suggests that strength is also largely unaffected by grain refinement induced by changes in cooling rates. This is consistent with our previous work that showed hardness varying modestly in a weld buildup made with 40kj/in heat input [ 21 ]. This finding highlights a key distinction of the Fe-10Ni weld metal. Such insensitivity offers a practical advantage for welding since a wider processing window can be tolerated without significant degradation in hardness. Additionally in martensite, hardness is controlled by the carbon content, with higher carbon content resulting in harder martensite [ 44 ]. One potential reason for the negligible variations in hardness due to grain size is the low carbon content in the weld metal. This results in a “soft” martensite and variations in hardness may not be as noticeable.

sections.heading: Impact toughness
paragraphs: In contrast to hardness, impact toughness exhibits a clearer dependence on grain size variations due to peak temperature. Figure  11  shows that impact toughness differs substantially between peak temperature conditions, with finer effective grain sizes associated with higher absorbed energy. The distinction between the 1000 °C and 1350 °C conditions highlights that peak temperature–driven grain coarsening has a more pronounced influence on toughness than cooling rate alone. Within a given peak temperature, variations in cooling rate produce measurable changes in effective grain size but result in only minor differences in CVN energies. The effective grain size associated with the lower peak temperature condition remains relatively small, resulting in similar impact toughness values regardless of cooling rate. In contrast, at the higher peak temperature condition, the effective grain size is already sufficiently coarse that further increases due to slower cooling do not lead to a comparable reduction in toughness. These observations suggest a threshold-type response, as shown in Fig.  12 , in which refinement below an effective grain size of approximately 3 µm results in a significant improvement in toughness, while further coarsening beyond this threshold has a comparatively limited effect. This behavior corresponds well with the conditions under which CM was observed. As discussed in Section 3.2, CM was identified at 1100 °C when cooling rates were below 38 °C/s, at 1200 °C when cooling rates were below 62 °C/s, and at 1350 °C across all investigated cooling rates. Examination of the effective grain sizes for these conditions (Fig.  4 b and Table  5 ) shows that they are all greater than 3 µm. In addition, the 1350 °C condition exhibited CM for both cooling rates evaluated, which may explain the lack of a noticeable difference in CVN impact energies between these conditions.

EBSD characterization along the fracture surface provides additional insight into these differences in fracture behavior (Fig.  13 ). The finer grain structure associated with the 1000 °C condition is clear and confirms the effectiveness of the applied thermal simulations. KAM analysis indicates a higher average local misorientation in the 1000 °C condition compared to the 1350 °C condition. The increased KAM reflects a greater accumulation of plastic strain before fracture, which is consistent with the higher absorbed CVN energy measured for this condition. Similar relationships between increased misorientation accumulation and improved impact toughness have been reported in steels, where greater plastic work is required to advance the crack through a refined microstructure [ 45 ].

The as-welded condition exhibited the worst CVN energies, due to the largest PAG and effective grain sizes, as shown in Figs.  5  and  6 . This indicates that in multipass welding, reheating to both low and high peak temperatures within the weld metal HAZ promotes microstructural refinement relative to the as-welded columnar structure, resulting in improved impact toughness. Previous work on Fe-10Ni weld metal has shown that as-welded regions that do not undergo sufficient reheating or reaustenitization are prone to cleavage fracture, a morphology typically associated with low impact toughness [ 10 ]. Barrick and DuPont further concluded that the persistence of as-welded regions in multipass GMAW Fe-10Ni welds, together with their larger grain sizes and CM presence, contributes to their lower impact toughness compared to GTAW welds.

sections.heading: Absence of carbide grain boundary pinning
paragraphs: The limited grain growth observed at lower peak temperatures prompted evaluation of potential grain boundary pinning mechanisms. Given the deliberate addition of vanadium to the consumable composition [ 9 ], vanadium carbide formation represents a plausible grain refinement mechanism in low carbon steels through Zener pinning [ 13 ,  27 ]. Carbon replica analysis was therefore employed to assess the presence of fine carbides at a smaller length scale (Fig.  14 ). Although numerous particles were recovered, TEM and STEM-EDS analysis identified these particles as oxides rather than carbides. This observation is consistent with the low carbon content of the weld metal, which limits carbide formation. The absence of VC and other carbides indicates that grain growth resistance at lower peak temperatures arises from limited diffusion kinetics and restricted grain boundary mobility near the A C3  temperature, rather than from carbide-based pinning. Elemental mapping further revealed that oxides incorporate vanadium and molybdenum, potentially reducing the availability of these elements for grain refinement while simultaneously increasing the density of void nucleation sites during impact loading. This dual role highlights the importance of controlling oxide content in Fe-10Ni weld metal to optimize both grain structure and impact toughness.

sections.heading: Summary and conclusions
paragraphs: This study investigated the influence of reaustenization on the grain refinement mechanism, martensitic substructure, and mechanical properties in multipass Fe-10Ni weld metal, using controlled isothermal and non-isothermal thermal simulations, metallurgical characterization, hardness, and Charpy impact testing. Analysis of the obtained results led to the following conclusions: Supercritical reheating of as-solidified Fe-10Ni weld metal significantly refined the original coarse -grained dendritic microstructure by forming small equiaxed grains. Reaustenization of the tested weld metal reduced the average PAG size with about two orders of magnitude, refined up to four times the effective grain size, and increased the HAGB density from approximately 0.20 μm to 0.86 μm1 in the most refined condition, produced by 1000 °C reheat and 62 °C/s cooling rate. The extent of grain refinement was controlled by the peak reaustenization temperatures and dwell times above the AC3 temperature. Short reaustenization at 1000 °C reduced the original PAG size from 570 μm to 12 μm and the effective grain size from 10 μm to 2.3 μm. Comparatively lower degree of grain refinement, to PAG size of 81 μm and effective grain size of 6.3 μm, occurred at 1350 °C reaustenization and a cooling rate representative of higher heat input GMAW processes. Subsequent supercritical and intercritical reheats of simulated CGHAZ reduced the PAG size back to 17 μm and the effective grain size back to 2.6 μm. The kinetics of grain size evolution during austenitization is governed by diffusionmediated grain boundary migration rather than carbide grain boundary pinning. This was evidenced by the slow grain growth at isothermal holding and by the absence of carbides in the Fe-10Ni weld metal. The latter was related to the low weld metal carbon content and the carbide formers, V and Mo, being tied in weld metal oxide particles. A critical HAGB density threshold of approximately 0.57 μm1 was identified, below which coarse martensite constituents were present in supercritically reheated Fe-10Ni weld metal. This HAGB density corresponded to PAG size and effective grain size, respectively, exceeding 31 μm and 3 μm. Coarse martensite was also observed in the as-welded condition. The Fe–10Ni weld metal hardness is relatively insensitive to reaustenization reheats. Despite measurable differences in PAG and effective grain size in the reaustenitized weld metal, hardness remained within a narrow range of 303 to 325 HV0.2. This behavior was attributed to the low carbon content of the alloy, which produces relatively soft martensite and reduces hardness sensitivity to grain size variations. Simulated single-reheat weld metal HAZ demonstrated notable improvement in the CVN impact energy of the tested Fe-10Ni weld metal. This improvement can be attributed to the significantly refined equiaxed grain microstructure and higher HAGB density in the reaustenitized weld metal compared to the as-welded condition. In contrast to the 1350 °C reheats, the better performance of 1000 °C specimens was related to the higher than critical HAGB densities and absence of coarse martensite constituents in the microstructure. These effects were also indicated by higher level of plastic strain along the fracture surface of a CVN test specimen reaustenitized at 1000 °C. In future work, additional hardness and CVN testing utilizing Design of Experiments (DoE) strategies across a broader range of simulated cooling rates and peak temperatures would further strengthen confidence in the observed trends.
